title: Merge sort
summary: Divide and conquer: split, sort the halves, merge.

cards.title: Divide and conquer
cards.body:
Sorting 8 values is hard. Sorting 1 value is free: it's already sorted.

**Merge sort** keeps splitting the list in half until each piece has one value. Then it **merges** pieces back together, two sorted halves at a time.

cards.title: Merging is easy
cards.body:
Two sorted piles: `[2, 5]` and `[1, 9]`. Look at the top of each, take the smaller one, repeat.

1 (from right), 2 (left), 5 (left), 9 (right). Done: `[1, 2, 5, 9]`. Each value is looked at once.
The underlined window is the range being worked on. Green flashes mean "this range is merged and sorted".

cards.title: The code
cards.body:
The function calls **itself** on each half. That's **recursion**. The base case `hi - lo < 2` stops it.

`[lo, hi)` means lo is included and hi is not, exactly like `begin()`/`end()` in the STL. It makes the maths with sizes clean.

cards.title: Why O(n log n)?
cards.body:
Halving 8 values gives 3 levels of splits (8 → 4 → 2 → 1). In general that's **log₂ n** levels.

On each level, merging touches all n values once. n work × log n levels = **O(n log n)**. For a million values: ~20 million steps instead of bubble sort's ~500 billion.

The cost: merging needs an extra buffer of n values, so **O(n) extra memory**.

cards.question: You have 1,024 values. How many levels of halving does merge sort need to reach single values?
Merge sort's worst case on 1,000 values is roughly...
cards.explain: n log n ≈ 1,000 × 10. Unlike quicksort, merge sort has no bad inputs. Its worst case is still O(n log n).
